Name: distributed_harm_aggregation
Title: Safety Reads Only the Last Word: Jailbreaks as Read-Out Aggregation Failures and a Distributed Harm-Evidence Monitor
Short Hypothesis: Safety-aligned LLMs make the refuse/comply decision by reading harm signal at essentially a single aggregation point (the prompt's final position), yet the evidence that a request is harmful is distributed across many earlier token positions in the residual stream. Jailbreaks succeed largely by preventing that distributed harm evidence from being routed into the final-position read-out, even while the harm signal remains legibly present at earlier positions. Therefore, a monitor that integrates the latent harm signal across ALL prompt positions—rather than reading one position—will detect jailbroken harmful requests far more robustly than the model's own refusal or a single-position probe.
Related Work: Shallow-alignment work (Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis, Li & Kim 2024; 'When Autoregressive Consistency Hurts Safety Alignment' 2026) shows safety updates concentrate on early *output* tokens; we instead study *prompt* token positions and the read-out geometry, not output-trajectory consistency. Refusal-direction work (Arditi et al.; Pan et al. ICML 2025; Zhao et al. NeurIPS 2025) extracts a direction but reads it at a single (last) prompt token and never asks whether harm evidence exists at other positions or whether aggregation is the point of failure. ConceptGuard (2025) uses SAEs for shared jailbreak geometry but still classifies at pooled representations without a position-resolved harm-evidence account. SafeSeek/SafeSeek-style circuit work localizes components, not positional read-out. Our distinction: we reframe jailbreak vulnerability as a *read-out aggregation failure*—the harm representation is intact and position-distributed, but attacks disrupt its routing to the decision position—and we exploit position-resolved harm decoding to build a training-free, position-aggregating monitor.
Abstract: Mechanistic accounts localize LLM refusal to a low-dimensional direction, but this direction is almost always read at a single position: the prompt's final token, where the decision is made. We ask a simple question with large consequences: where does the *evidence* of harm actually live, and is the safety decision a faithful aggregation of it? We construct a position-resolved harm probe and show that on genuinely harmful prompts, a decodable harm signal is distributed across many token positions in the residual stream, peaking near harm-bearing content words rather than only at the final position. We then analyze diverse jailbreaks (GCG suffixes, roleplay/DAN, low-resource translation, prefix-injection, distractor-padding) and find a consistent phenomenon: the per-position harm signal at the harm-bearing tokens remains largely intact, but its projection into the final decision position collapses—attacks succeed by disrupting routing/aggregation, not by erasing the harm representation. This diagnosis, validated with attention- and patching-based routing analyses, motivates a training-free defense: a monitor that pools the harm signal across all prompt positions (max/attention-weighted aggregation) instead of trusting the single decision position. Across Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, the distributed-aggregation monitor detects jailbroken harmful requests with substantially higher AUROC and lower benign false-positive rate than the model's own refusal, a single-position probe, and output-based guardrails, and generalizes to held-out attacks. We recast a large class of jailbreaks from 'defeating the safety representation' to 'defeating its read-out,' and show the read-out is the cheaper thing to fix.
Experiments: 1) Position-resolved harm probe: on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, fit a linear harm probe (difference-in-means / logistic on harmful vs benign) using residual activations at EACH prompt token position (not just the last). Establish that on clean harmful prompts the harm-signal projection is elevated at multiple positions (especially harm-bearing content tokens), quantified by per-position projection profiles and the fraction of total harm evidence outside the final position. Validate probe with paraphrase and cross-category generalization. 2) Aggregation-failure diagnosis: apply 5 jailbreak families (GCG, roleplay/DAN, low-resource translation, prefix-injection, distractor-padding) to harmful prompts from AdvBench/HarmBench/StrongREJECT. For each, measure (a) the per-position harm projection at the original harm-bearing tokens vs (b) the harm projection at the final decision position. Hypothesis: (a) stays high while (b) collapses. Report the 'aggregation gap' per attack family. 3) Routing analysis: use attention patterns and activation patching to test whether attacks reduce attention/information flow from harm-bearing positions to the final position; patch the harm-bearing-position activations into the jailbroken final position and measure whether refusal is restored (causal test of the routing/aggregation hypothesis). 4) Distributed-aggregation monitor: build a training-free monitor that pools the per-position harm projections across all prompt tokens via (i) max, (ii) top-k mean, (iii) attention-weighted pooling; flag if pooled score exceeds a threshold calibrated on a held-out mixed set. Compare jailbreak-detection AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, and benign false-positive rate against: (a) the standard single-final-position refusal probe, (b) the model's own refusal decision, (c) Llama-Guard on the output, (d) perplexity input filter, (e) mean-pooled (non-harm-aware) representation baseline. 5) Over-refusal control: evaluate the monitor on XSTest and OR-Bench to ensure distributed pooling does not fire on benign trigger-word prompts; report over-refusal rate. 6) Generalization: leave-one-attack-out and cross-model transfer of the position-resolved probe and monitor. Metrics: per-position harm profiles, aggregation gap per attack, causal patching effect sizes, monitor AUROC/TPR@FPR/FPR, over-refusal rate, cross-attack/model transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) On some attacks (e.g., low-resource translation or cipher obfuscation) the harm signal may genuinely be erased at ALL positions rather than merely un-aggregated, in which case the distributed monitor cannot help—this per-attack characterization is itself an informative contribution and delineates 'representation-defeating' vs 'read-out-defeating' attacks. 2) Distributed pooling could increase benign false positives on prompts that mention harm-adjacent words; the XSTest/OR-Bench over-refusal control directly tests and bounds this, and top-k/attention pooling is designed to mitigate it. 3) The single-position vs multi-position distinction may be smaller than hypothesized in some models; we test three families and report effect heterogeneity. 4) Position-resolved probes can latch onto surface lexical features; we control with paraphrase, cross-category, and leave-one-attack-out generalization. 5) The causal patching test may be confounded by activation-distribution mismatch across positions; we use matched-norm and placebo-position controls. 6) Results are on mid-size open-weight models with standard decoding; frontier transfer is untested, though the read-out-aggregation framing is model-agnostic.
